Meeting header:
Title: Edge-case walkthrough: concurrent sessions, cache eviction & streaming shedding
Date/Time: 2026-10-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Leo Park (Redwood SE), Alice Moreno (Meridian SRE), Tom Rivers (Meridian CTO), Samir Patel (Meridian ML), Rachel Li (Meridian Security)

Summary (auto): quick demo of Redwood runtime behavior under combined long-context + high TPS load. Focus areas: KV/prefix cache eviction behavior, streaming backpressure and shedding, session timeouts and handoff, fallback to smaller model variants, and security questions around logs/KMS.
Topics: long context handling (64k+), sustained high TPS (1k+), streaming backpressure, client-side timeouts, canary/fallback config, SOC2/KMS questions

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, welcome, thanks for joining. we, uh, are gonna run through a few edge cases you hit in your notes — long sessions + high tps and some streaming backpressure. priya and leo from our se team are with me.
[00:18] Alice (Meridian): hey, thanks. to be clear, we saw two things in prod last month: long customer sessions that kept growing memory, and during busy windows our streaming clients start getting partial chunks and then time out, clients retry and we see a surge.
[00:33] Priya (Redwood SE): yeah, that's common when prefix caching and KV cache eviction interact with session reuse. quick show of hands: are you primarily using our hosted api or dedicated pools?
[00:44] Tom (Meridian): dedicated right now — reserved gpus in a private vpc. we like the isolation. but we do have an internal svc that opens ~3k concurrent websockets across sessions.
[00:55] Samir (Meridian): and context lengths: some flows go out to ~80k tokens because we stitch a full conversation plus document history. we know that pushes kernel memory up.
[01:10] Leo (Redwood SE): okay that's helpful. two quick notes: our runtime supports 64k and 128k model variants, but higher context can change batching dynamics. also the KV cache we keep per-session has a TTL and an eviction LRU when memory pressure hits. evictions can cause the runtime to recompute keys which temporarily raises latency and can conflict with streaming backpressure windows.
[01:32] Alice: when eviction happens we saw p95 jump from ~220ms to 1.4s and then clients sometimes retry. is there a way to avoid that spike?
[01:42] Priya: a few levers — prefix caching (persist frequently accessed prefixes to a separate LRU with longer TTL), configuring max sequence length per model to avoid loading full 128k when not needed, and using model routing: e.g. put long-session users on an autoscaled, high-memory pool and short chat on cheaper ones. also we can make evictions asynchronous more gracefully so streaming doesn't block.
[02:05] Tom: can you elaborate on "asynchronous" — like how does streaming behave while the kernel recomputes kvs? we observed instead that some streams stop sending chunks and the connection resets.
[02:16] Priya: right — today the default is best-effort: if the runtime hits backpressure it will attempt to keep the stream open and emit what it has, but if buffers exceed thresholds we apply shedding — respond with an internal error or a restart token depending on config. you can tune the thresholds per route.
[02:34] Samir: is that the same as a 503? sometimes our clients see a 200 with truncated output.
[02:39] Leo: yeah, implementation detail depends on the client binding. HTTP streaming via chunked will often finish with a final boundary but with a shorter reply. websocket flows we can send a "partial_response" event then a "retry_token" so client can continue from prefix. the shorter/truncated 200 is usually when a preflight filter on the client ODM cuts the response.
[03:01] Jordan: i want to show a quick run — we prepared a short demo using a synthetic workload that mimics your session shapes. priya will drive.
[03:08] Priya: hitting the demo now. (screen-share) ok — scenario A: 1.2k TPS sustained, median ctx 18k tokens, a tail of 80k; we start with an initial warm cache and then inject a hot pattern to cause evictions. watch p95 and streaming behavior.
[03:30] [sound of typing]
[03:42] Priya: you can see at minute 6 the LRU eviction % jumps, and at the same time streaming chunk intervals increase. client retransmits spiked.
[03:55] Alice: that's similar to our logs. curious — the graph shows "fallthrough model switchover" at minute 7, what is that?
[04:04] Priya: good eye — that's our configured fallback policy: if a high-memory variant is saturated, we route new requests to a lower-memory compatible model (faster, smaller context), and we tag it with a fallback flag so app logic can choose to re-request a full generation offline. it prevents total outage but does change quality.
[04:23] Tom: and do you have metrics that show how often that happens vs just queuing? we don't want silent fallbacks causing user-visible regressions.
[04:31] Leo: yes — every fallback emits a trace with reason and decision tree; Console has a per-route dashboard that shows fallback rate, latency delta, and cost impact. you can set hard SLOs to prevent fallback outside maintenance windows.
[04:46] Samir: about streaming backpressure — can Redwood buffer more on the server side instead of asking clients to retry? we have expensive client-side state machines that don't retry gracefully.
[04:56] Priya: you can increase server buffer thresholds but that increases memory and can exacerbate evictions. another approach: enable progressive flushing — send partial tokens earlier and let the client reconstruct; or use a passthrough mode where we stream to a proxy that handles retransmit, we have a reference proxy in our docs.
[05:16] Alice: is that proxy included in dedicated? we'd prefer not to operate another component.
[05:21] Jordan: we can run the proxy as part of the dedicated deployment as an optional sidecar managed by Redwood for enterprise customers. for Private/VPC installs we provide the image and runbook.
[05:33] Rachel (Security): quick security Q — when you mention buffer persistence and fallback tokens, are those persisted to disk or encrypted in memory? we need to know for compliance.
[05:43] Leo: buffers are in-memory; if you enable persistent prefix cache to accelerate cold-starts we can persist encrypted entries to the customer KMS/HSM in your account — Redwood does not hold plaintext. we also emit audit logs for evictions and access; those logs can be sent to your SIEM.
[05:58] Rachel: ok please send the KMS integration doc.
[06:02] Jordan: noted — will add to next steps.
[06:08] Priya: now jumping to timeouts — clients often set a hard 30s request timeout. when a long context triggers recompute, you'd exceed that. two mitigations: increase client-side timeout for long sessions; enable an early-ack that returns a retry_token so clients know to poll; or use a streaming heartbeat to keep connection alive.
[06:29] Samir: our mobile clients are picky — we don't want long polling. is there a way to offload long jobs to a queued async path with webhook callback?
[06:36] Priya: yes, Redwood supports async request/response — we can enqueue a job on Dedicated and notify via webhook or webhook+S3 payload. good for heavy document synthesis where UX can be async.
[06:48] Alice: what about session handoff? we do sudden worker restarts and want sessions to continue when a user reconnects to a different backend.
[06:56] Leo: we have a session token scheme where the KV cache can be checkpointed and rehydrated; checkpointing frequency is tunable. rehydration time depends on context size — for large sequences we recommend incremental checkpointing and a warm pool for rehydration to keep p95 under target.
[07:15] Tom: can you show the console flags where we set the thresholds?
[07:20] Priya: sure. (screen-share Console) route config -> advanced -> streaming buffer threshold, fallback policy, cache TTLs. you can also configure an autoscaling rule that increases high-memory nodes when eviction rate > 3% for 5m.
[07:40] Alice: i see a config for "shed_mode": drop | retry_token | block. what's recommended?
[07:46] Leo: for financial workflows we usually recommend retry_token so client can reattach and you keep auditability. drop is for best-effort low-cost flows. block is strict — it will hold until memory pressure resolves which can cause head-of-line blocking.
[08:00] Samir: one more question on kernel selection: when you say switching to smaller model, does that require re-tokenization or can you change mid-stream?
[08:09] Priya: switching model mid-stream is expensive — we do a graceful switchover: we finish the current token batch, emit a marker in the stream, and then subsequent requests target the other model. re-tokenization is handled server-side; we expose a retry_token that indicates a model-change occurred.
[08:27] Tom: we need SLAs on latency for p95 even during peak. can dedicated provide by-reservation latency SLOs?
[08:34] Jordan: yes, Dedicated offers predictable throughput and latency SLOs in contracts. we back them with reserved GPUs and options for burst capacity. for long-tail workloads we recommend a hybrid: reserved for critical paths and hosted for burst overflow.
[08:47] Alice: i want to call out an incident: during our last run we had a cascading retry loop — clients retried on truncated 200s, overwhelmed the queue and caused more evictions. how do we break that loop?
[08:58] Leo: circuit-breaker + jittered exponential backoff on client helps. also server side we can add adaptive rate limiting per-identity and a small queue that prioritizes non-retrying sessions. the Console lets you profile per-token costs so you can see the cost impact of retries.
[09:17] Samir: for the PoC we'd like you to run a controlled 48-hour stress test with our workload and collect: p50/p95/p99 latency, fallback rate, eviction rate, streaming truncation events, and memory pressure.
[09:28] Priya: that's doable. we'll need a sample workload and access to a staging VPC. we'll propose instance sizing and a test plan.
[09:35] Jordan: quick recap — action items and deliverables noted. any final quick questions?
[09:42] Tom: are there pricing implications for turning on persistent prefix cache and the sidecar proxy?
[09:47] Jordan: yes — those are opt-in features that change cost. we'll include pricing bands in the sheet. persistent cache is metered by storage and throughput. proxy sidecars are on dedicated nodes.
[09:58] Rachel: also we need the SOC2 and KMS docs before the PoC.
[10:02] Jordan: we'll send those.

[10:05] Priya (closing demo): thanks everyone — i'll follow up with the runbook and the canary plan, jordan will send pricing.
[10:12] Alice: thank you, this was useful.
